title: Heterogeneous graphs & relation types
blurb: Multiple node/edge types, relation types, when types are not just features

hook.title: A city with many kinds of roads
hook.text: Picture a city where **people**, **shops** and **offices** are connected by *different kinds* of roads: friendships, deliveries, commutes. A “road” between a person and a shop means something very different from one between two people. A **heterogeneous graph** keeps the kinds explicit: a *relation type* is the triple (where the road starts, what kind of road, where it ends). You could just stamp a label on each node and edge and pretend it's one big map, but sometimes the kinds need different instruments altogether.
hook.recall: Remember the city of many roads: a relation type is (start type, edge type, end type). Types can be one-hot features, unless the types need different feature shapes or different models.

explore.intro: Choose how many node and edge types exist.
tasks: Set 2 node types and 2 edge types. How many possible relation types? Compare with the slide.
Switch to *one-hot type features*. When would this simplification fail?
explore.takeaway: $G=(V,E,\tau,\phi)$; $r(u,v)=(\tau(u),\phi(u,v),\tau(v))$. Two node types × two edge types gives 8 possible relation types. A heterogeneous graph is more expressive but costs more computation, storage and implementation complexity.

build.prompt: Complete the definition of a relation type.

questions.prompt: A graph has 2 node types (Paper, Author) and 2 edge types (Cite, Like). How many possible relation types $(\text{node\_start},\text{edge},\text{node\_end})$ are there?
In a heterogeneous graph $G=(V,E,\tau,\phi)$, what is $\phi$?
options: The edge-type function: $\phi(u,v)$ gives the type of edge $(u,v)$

questions.prompt: Which is a case where we **need** a true heterogeneous graph rather than one-hot type features?
options: Author nodes have 4-dim features, paper nodes 5-dim features
All nodes have the same features
questions.explanation: Different shapes of features per type can’t share one input layer. (Another case: relations that need different models.)

options: Types can be treated as features by appending a one-hot indicator to nodes and edges
A heterogeneous graph can capture different types of interactions between entities
A heterogeneous graph costs the same as a homogeneous graph
Relation types capture the interaction between nodes and edges better than node types alone
questions.explanation: It is more expressive but more expensive (computation, storage) and more complex to implement.

questions.prompt: (English, translate, French) and (English, translate, Chinese) are two relations. Why might they deserve different models?
options: They represent different types of interactions
Because they have the same features
questions.explanation: Case 2 on slide 9: different relation types represent different interactions.

questions.prompt: *“Appending one-hot type indicators always makes a heterogeneous graph exactly equivalent to a homogeneous one, so we never need heterogeneous GNNs.”* What’s wrong?
options: It reduces to a homogeneous graph only superficially; when types have different feature shapes or need different models, explicit heterogeneous handling is needed
questions.explanation: Stamping labels on the map doesn’t give the roads different instruments.
